prompt: What does a histogram show that a bar chart of categories does not?

choices.why: That is a bar chart's job.

choices.text: How two quantities are related to each other
choices.why: Two quantities together want a scatterplot, lesson 6.
Time is a line chart's axis.
Right. That spread is the distribution.

prompt: Why do a histogram's bars touch?

choices.text: To save space on the page
choices.why: The gaps would cost little. The touching carries meaning.
Categories get gaps; the bins of a quantity do not.

choices.text: Each bin ends where the next begins
choices.why: Right. The axis is one continuous quantity cut into pieces.

choices.text: So the reader can add the counts more easily
choices.why: Adding counts is no easier with touching bars.

prompt: A histogram of delivery times shows two separate peaks. What is the likeliest explanation?

choices.why: Right. Bicycles and vans, or two depots, would do it.
Wide bins merge peaks; they rarely create a second one.

choices.text: Most deliveries took the average time
choices.why: With two peaks the average may sit between them, where few deliveries are.

choices.text: The data is skewed to the right
choices.why: Skew is one peak with a long tail.

prompt: Delivery times have a long right tail. Which single number describes the typical delivery better?

choices.why: The few very slow deliveries drag it upwards.
That describes the worst delivery, not the typical one.
Right. The mean is pulled towards the tail.

choices.text: The range from smallest to largest
choices.why: The range describes the extremes, not the middle.

prompt: A histogram with very narrow bins shows many small spikes and dips. What are they most likely to be?

choices.why: They would survive a wider bin if they were.
Right. With few values per bin, a few more or less is chance.
The values can be perfectly correct and still look ragged in narrow bins.
Groups make a few clear peaks, not dozens of small spikes.

prompt: Moving where the bins start, with the same width, changed the shape of the histogram. What should you conclude?

choices.why: Neither start is more correct than the other.
The data did not change at all.

choices.text: Trust only the features that survive several starts
choices.why: Right. A feature that vanishes when the edges move was made by the edges.
They can, once a few settings have been tried.

prompt: Which bin edges does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Round numbers that are easy to say
choices.why: Right. 5, 10, 15 minutes; R$ 10 bands.

choices.text: Exactly the edges the formula returns, such as 23.7 to 28.6
choices.why: Nobody can talk about a bin from 23.7 to 28.6.

choices.text: Edges that put the same number of values in every bin
choices.why: That makes every bar the same height and hides the shape.

choices.text: Edges starting at the smallest value in the data
choices.why: That gives odd edges like 12.2, 17.2 and so on.

prompt: How many bins does the square-root rule suggest for 400 values?
Why did Sturges's rule suggest too few bins for Horta's deliveries?

choices.text: It counts only the values above the median
choices.why: It uses the number of values, all of them.

choices.text: It was written for categories rather than quantities
choices.why: It is a rule for histograms of quantities.

choices.text: 400 values is too few for any rule
choices.why: The other two rules gave sensible widths for the same 400.

choices.text: It assumes a bell shape, and this data is skewed
choices.why: Right. Its 10 bins of almost 9 minutes look like the blocky picture.

prompt: Why is Freedman–Diaconis better than a rule based on the full range when one delivery took 101 minutes?

choices.why: Nothing is removed; the extreme is still drawn.

choices.text: It uses the middle half of the data, so one extreme cannot widen every bin
choices.why: Right. The interquartile range ignores the tail.
Here it produced 26.

choices.text: It uses the mean instead of the median
choices.why: It uses quartiles, which are like the median, not the mean.

prompt: The quartiles of the delivery times were 27.00 and 39.82 minutes. What is the interquartile range, to two decimal places?
In a histogram with unequal bins, what must each bar's height be?

choices.why: Drawn by count, a wide bin looks like a crowd.

choices.text: Its count divided by its width
choices.why: Right. Then the area is the count, which is what the eye reads.
Width alone says nothing about how many values fell in it.

choices.text: The share of all values, as a percentage
choices.why: A percentage is still a count in disguise; it needs dividing by the width too.

prompt: The bin from 50 to 105 minutes holds 33 deliveries. What is its density, in deliveries per minute, to two decimal places?
Which axis title fits a histogram drawn by density?

choices.why: That would claim the height is a count.
Minutes are the horizontal axis.
A share is not divided by the width.
Right. Density is a rate, and the axis should say so.

prompt: Which view answers "what share of deliveries took under 45 minutes?" most directly?

choices.why: You would have to add up every bar below 45.
A pie of times would need bins and still show only shares of those bins.
Right. Up from 45 to the curve, across to the axis.
You would have to count the dots.

prompt: A density curve has no bins. What setting does it hide instead?

choices.why: Right. It behaves exactly like the bin width.

choices.text: The starting point of the axis
choices.why: The axis range is a separate matter.
That is the data, not a setting.

choices.text: Nothing; it has no settings at all
choices.why: Its smoothness is a choice, and a wrong one misleads.

prompt: You have 50,000 delivery times. Why is a strip of dots a poor choice?

choices.text: The dots merge into a smear
choices.why: Right. Beyond a few hundred values, a histogram or a density curve does better.
It has none; that is its advantage at small sizes.
Extremes are what it shows best, as single dots.

choices.text: Jitter changes the values it draws
choices.why: Jitter moves dots off the axis, never along it.
